title: The Exoplanet Being Torn Apart By Its Star
description: Journey to WASP-12b, an exoplanet so close to its star that it's literally being ripped apart, glowing like an ember. 🔥 Discover the extreme forces and ultimate fate of this cosmic anomaly. What other wonders does the universe hide? 🤔
script:
Imagine a world where the very fabric of planetary existence is challenged, a celestial body defying our intuitive understanding of gravitational stability. Far from the serene, spherical planets of our solar system, there exists an exoplanet that presents a mind-bending paradox, a "glitch in physics" that makes us question the resilience of worlds.

This isn't a theoretical construct but a documented reality: the exoplanet WASP-12b. Discovered in 2008, WASP-12b is a gas giant located approximately 1,200 light-years away in the constellation Auriga. It belongs to a class of exoplanets known as "hot Jupiters" – massive, gaseous worlds orbiting exceptionally close to their parent stars. But WASP-12b takes this proximity to an unprecedented, almost suicidal extreme.

Orbiting its star, WASP-12, at a mere 3.4 million kilometers (2.1 million miles) – just 1/44th the distance between Earth and the Sun – WASP-12b completes a full revolution in a staggering 1.12 Earth days. This intense gravitational embrace has profound consequences. The star's immense tidal forces are literally tearing the planet apart. Like a cosmic tug-of-war, the gravitational pull on the side of WASP-12b closest to its star is significantly stronger than on the far side, stretching the planet into a distinctly non-spherical, oblate spheroid shape, often likened to a cosmic American football. This distortion is so pronounced that its equatorial radius is estimated to be twice its polar radius.

The extreme proximity also subjects WASP-12b to unimaginable temperatures. Its day side can reach scorching temperatures of up to 2,500 degrees Celsius (4,532 degrees Fahrenheit), hot enough to vaporize most metals. Under these conditions, the planet's hydrogen-rich atmosphere is not merely hot; it's superheated to the point of glowing. Scientists have observed that its atmosphere absorbs so much stellar radiation that it appears like a burning ember, radiating an intense red light visible across vast cosmic distances. This atmospheric glow is a direct consequence of the thermal emission from extremely hot gas.

Further observations by the Hubble Space Telescope revealed that WASP-12b is not just distorted but actively being consumed by its star. Its outer atmosphere is rapidly expanding and spilling onto the star, forming a massive, comet-like tail of escaping planetary material. It's estimated that WASP-12b is losing mass at an astonishing rate of about 189 quadrillion tons per year, equivalent to three Earth masses every 10 million years. This stellar cannibalism means WASP-12b has a finite, relatively short lifespan, predicted to be only another 10 million years before it is completely absorbed.

This dying world offers astronomers a unique laboratory to study extreme planetary dynamics, atmospheric escape, and the ultimate fate of planets caught in a death spiral with their stars. Beyond its physical demise, WASP-12b also presents intriguing atmospheric properties, with some models suggesting it might be a "carbon planet" with an atmosphere rich in carbon compounds rather than oxygen, leading to exotic chemistry, potentially forming diamonds deep within its interior. WASP-12b is a stark, incandescent reminder of the brutal, dynamic processes that shape the universe, a world not just existing, but dramatically fading, one atom at a time, into the heart of its hungry parent star.
